title: Making Multicurves Cross Minimally on Surfaces
abstract:
On an orientable surface S, consider a collection Γ of closed curves. The (geometric) intersection number i_S(Γ) is the minimum number of self-intersections that a collection Γ' can have, where Γ' results from a continuous deformation (homotopy) of Γ. We provide algorithms that compute i_S(Γ) and such a Γ', assuming that Γ is given by a collection of closed walks of length n in a graph M cellularly embedded on S, in O(n log n) time when M and S are fixed.
The state of the art is a paper of Despré and Lazarus [SoCG 2017, J. ACM 2019], who compute i_S(Γ) in O(n²) time, and Γ' in O(n⁴) time if Γ is a single closed curve. Our result is more general since we can put an arbitrary number of closed curves in minimal position. Also, our algorithms are quasi-linear in n instead of quadratic and quartic. Most importantly, our proofs are simpler, shorter, and more structured.
We use techniques from two-dimensional topology and from the theory of hyperbolic surfaces. Most notably, we prove a new property of the reducing triangulations introduced by Colin de Verdière, Despré, and Dubois [SODA 2024], reducing our problem to the case of surfaces with boundary. As a key subroutine, we rely on an algorithm of Fulek and Tóth [JCO 2020].

      Abstract
On an orientable surface S, consider a collection Γ of closed curves. The (geometric) intersection
number iS (Γ) is the minimum number of self-intersections that a collection Γ′ can have, where Γ′
results from a continuous deformation (homotopy) of Γ. We provide algorithms that compute iS (Γ)
and such a Γ′ , assuming that Γ is given by a collection of closed walks of length n in a graph M
cellularly embedded on S, in O(n log n) time when M and S are fixed.
    The state of the art is a paper of Despré and Lazarus [SoCG 2017, J. ACM 2019], who compute
iS (Γ) in O(n2 ) time, and Γ′ in O(n4 ) time if Γ is a single closed curve. Our result is more general
since we can put an arbitrary number of closed curves in minimal position. Also, our algorithms are
quasi-linear in n instead of quadratic and quartic. Most importantly, our proofs are simpler, shorter,
and more structured.
    We use techniques from two-dimensional topology and from the theory of hyperbolic surfaces.
Most notably, we prove a new property of the reducing triangulations introduced by Colin de
Verdière, Despré, and Dubois [SODA 2024], reducing our problem to the case of surfaces with
boundary. As a key subroutine, we rely on an algorithm of Fulek and Tóth [JCO 2020].

 1      Introduction
The problem
On a surface S, a collection Γ of closed curves is in general position if no point of S is
the image of more than two points of Γ, and if every self-intersection of Γ is a crossing.
In addition, Γ is in minimal position if no continuous deformation, in other words no
homotopy, can decrease its number of crossings. The (geometric) intersection number
iS (Γ) is the number of crossings of a curve in minimal position homotopic to Γ. In this paper,
we provide algorithms for the following problems: given a collection Γ of closed curves on a
surface S, compute iS (Γ), and construct a collection Γ′ in minimal position, homotopic to Γ.
First, we review previous works.

Previous works
The intersection number of closed curves on surfaces was first studied by the mathematical
community. The problem of determining if a given closed curve is homotopic to a simple
(injective) one was studied by Poincaré [22], more recently by Reinhart [23], Chillingworth [7,

       8], and Birman and Series [3]. Later, Cohen and Lustig [9] and Lustig [21] (see also Hass
       and Scott [17]) determined the intersection number of one or two closed curves. De Graaf
       and Schrijver [12], and independently Hass and Scott [18], found out that closed curves can
       be put in minimal position via homotopy moves that never increase the number of crossings.
           It emerges from these studies that, among the orientable surfaces, those of genus g ≥ 2
       without boundary constitute the hardest cases. Also, if a collection Γ′ of closed curves is in
       minimal position, then every closed curve in Γ′ , and every pair of closed curves in Γ′ is also
       in minimal position [15, Section 1.2.4]. Thus, computing iS (Γ) for an arbitrary Γ boils down
       to computing iS (Γ) when Γ contains at most two closed curves. However, an algorithm that
       can put one or two closed curves in minimal position would not necessarily extend to an
       arbitrary number of closed curves.
           Recently, these problems have been revisited by computational topologists. The current
       state of the art is an algorithm provided by Despré and Lazarus [13] in a technical paper
       of 49 pages (see also Chang and De Mesmay [6] for the computation of homotopy moves
       that never increase the number of crossings). In the (popular) model they use, the input
       curves in Γ are specified up to homotopy by a collection of closed walks C in a graph M
       cellularly embedded on S, in that the faces of M all have genus zero and at most one
       boundary component. They proved:
       ▶ Theorem 1 (Despré, Lazarus, 2019). Let M be a graph of size m cellularly embedded on an
       orientable surface S. Let C be a collection of either one or two closed walks of total length n
       in M . One may compute iS (C) in O(m + n2 ) time.
            (The size of M is its number of edges.) When S has negative Euler characteristic, Despré
       and Lazarus also provide an algorithm to compute a closed curve γ ′ in minimal position,
       homotopic to a given closed walk C. They derive from M a quadrangulation Q, and return
       γ ′ as an “infinitesimal perturbation” of a closed walk C ′ in Q: in this paper, we say that γ ′
       is a perturbation of C ′ , and we leave this notion informal for now. They proved:
       ▶ Theorem 2 (Despré, Lazarus, 2019). Let M be a graph of size m cellularly embedded on an
       orientable surface S of negative Euler characteristic 1 . Let C be a closed walk of length n in
       M . One may construct in O(m + n4 ) time a quadrangulation Q, a closed walk C ′ of length
       O(n) in Q, homotopic to C, and a perturbation of C ′ with iS (C) self-crossings.
           We stress that Theorem 2 does not cope with more than one closed walk. Although
       Despré and Lazarus do not mention it, their output can easily be turned by isotopy into a
       perturbed closed walk of length O(mn) in M (instead of Q), at an additional cost of O(mn)
       time.
           A simpler problem is to consider only the perturbations of the input collection C of closed
       walks, instead of searching over all the collections C ′ homotopic to C, and to look for one
       with minimum self-crossing. This problem was studied by Fulek and Tóth [16] when the
       closed walks in C have no spur, that is, when they never take an edge of M and its reversal
       consecutively. They proved:
       ▶ Theorem 3 (Fulek, Tóth, 2020). Let M be an embedded graph of size m. Let C be a
       collection of closed walks of length n in M , without spur. One may construct a minimal
       perturbation of C in O(m + n log n) time.


       1

           negative. Indeed, their algorithm computes a “system of quads” [13, Section 8], a quadrangulation that
           is defined by them only when the Euler characteristic is negative [13, Section 4.2].

    The result of Fulek and Tóth has a different statement in their paper [16, Theorem 1]. In
particular, the embedded graph lies in the plane, and only one closed walk is given as input.
Nevertheless, Theorem 3 follows from their work.
    The problem of deciding whether a drawing of a graph on an orientable surface can be
untangled, in other words, whether it is homotopic to an injective map, was studied by Colin
de Verdière, Despré, and Dubois [10]. They provided a polynomial time algorithm. Along
the way, they introduced reducing triangulations. Every orientable surface of genus g ≥ 2
without boundary admits a reducing triangulation. A triangulation is reducing if its vertices
all have degree greater than or equal to eight, and if its dual graph is bipartite. Reducing
triangulations support reduced walks and reduced closed walks. Those are unique
among their homotopy class, are stable upon subwalk and reversal, and can be computed in
linear time from any given (closed) walk. Informally, they are convenient discrete analogs of
geodesics on hyperbolic surfaces.

Our results
We simplify, improve, and generalize the results of Despré and Lazarus. Naturally, we use the
same model for the input: a collection C of closed walks in a graph M cellularly embedded
on an orientable surface S. Our presentation focuses on the surfaces of genus g ≥ 2 without
boundary, as they constitute the hardest cases, but we prove similar results (with improved
complexities and simpler proofs) for the surfaces with boundary and the torus. The case of
the sphere is trivial. Here is the main result of the paper:

▶ Theorem 4. Let M be a graph of size m cellularly embedded on an orientable surface
S of genus g ≥ 2 without boundary. Let C be a collection of closed walks of length n
in M . One may compute iS (C) in O(m + g 2 + gn log(gn)) time. One may construct in
O(g 2 mn + gn log gn) time a collection C ′ of closed walks of length O(g 2 mn) in M , homotopic
to C, and a perturbation of C ′ with iS (C) self-crossings.

    We even deduce from Theorem 4 an algorithm of improved time complexity by allowing
for a more compact representation of the output curve (see Corollary 14), such as when
Despré and Lazarus return in a quadrangulation instead of M . Compared to Despré and
Lazarus, our result is more general since we can put an arbitrary number of closed curves in
minimal position. Also, our algorithms are quasi-linear in n instead of quadratic and quartic.
Most importantly, our proofs are simpler, shorter, and more structured as we benefit from
two recent tools that were not available to them: the result of Fulek and Tóth, and the
reducing triangulations of Colin de Verdière, Despré, and Dubois. A main contribution of
this paper is that it highlights the relationship between our problem and those tools.

Overview of the paper
After some preliminaries in Section 2, our starting point is the result of Fulek and Tóth,
Theorem 3. We observe (see Lemma 8) that in the setting of Theorem 3, if every face of M
contains a boundary component of S, then the returned perturbation of C has exactly iS (C)
self-crossings (not more). Motivated by this observation, we try to reduce our problem to an
application of Theorem 3. The difficulty is that, while spurs can trivially be eliminated from
the input closed walks, the faces of M do not generally contain a boundary component of S.
We overcome this difficulty by proving in Section 3 the following new property of reducing
triangulations:

       ▶ Proposition 5. Let T be a reducing triangulation of an orientable surface S of genus g ≥ 2
       without boundary. Let Σ be the surface obtained from S by removing an open disk from
       each face of T . Let C be a collection of reduced closed walks in the 1-skeleton of T . Then
       iS (C) = iΣ (C).

          Proposition 5 is largely inspired by [10, Proposition 4.3]. In Section 4, we combine
       Proposition 5 with the result of Fulek and Tóth (Theorem 3) to prove our main theorem,
       Theorem 4. Essentially, we observe that Theorem 4 is straightforward (with improved
       complexities even) when M is a reducing triangulation, and we handle the other cases with
       conversions between models adapted from [10, Section 7] (informally, we transform M into
       a reducing triangulation T , push C by homotopy in T , compute in T , and pull back the
       result in M ). In the same section, we handle the surfaces with boundary and the torus.
       Again, we reduce to an application of Theorem 3, but reducing triangulations are not needed
       anymore. For the surfaces with boundary, we only perform the conversions between models
       adapted from [10, Section 8]. For the torus, we define a particular kind of closed walks on a
       one-vertex embedded graph, for which we can prove a property similar to Proposition 5 (see
       Proposition 18).

        2      Preliminaries
       We assume some familiarity with basic notions of graph theory, and of the topology of surfaces.
       In this paper, every surface has finite type and is orientable, without further mention.

       2.1     Cellular embeddings
       A drawing of a graph M on a surface S is a map that sends the vertices of M to points
       of S, and the edges of M to paths between the corresponding endpoints. An embedding
       is an injective drawing. The faces of an embedding are the connected components of the
       complement of its image. An embedding is cellular if every face has genus zero and contains
       at most one boundary component. We briefly mention that there exist standard data
       structures to represent cellular graph embeddings on surfaces [14, 19].

       2.2     Lifting closed curves in the universal cover of a surface

       details, see, e.g., [2, Section 10.4].

       2.3     Hyperbolic surfaces
       We will use standard notions of two-dimensional hyperbolic geometry. See, e.g., Farb and
       Margalit [15, Chapter 1], also Cannon, Floyd, Kenyon, and Parry [5]. Our use of hyperbolic

(Bottom) The hyperbolic metric of Σ̊ is constructed by replacing the faces of Σ̊ by ideal hyperpolic

    A hyperbolic surface is a metric surface (here understood as a real, smooth two-
dimensional manifold equipped with a Riemannian metric) locally isometric to the hyperbolic
plane. Some hyperbolic surfaces can be constructed by considering ideal hyperbolic polygons,
the sides of which are complete (thus, of infinite length) geodesics, pairing the sides of the
polygons, and identifying every two paired sides in a way that respects the orientations
of the polygons. The topology of the resulting surface is that obtained by puncturing
(removing points from) a compact surface without boundary. Informally, the punctured
points correspond to infinitely long “spikes” of the metric.
    These surfaces enjoy the following specific properties: (1) There is a unique geodesic path
homotopic to any given path; (2) there is a unique geodesic closed curve freely homotopic
to any given closed curve, provided that curve is non-contractible and not homotopic to a
neighborhood of a puncture. Translating those properties into a discrete setting motivates
the introduction of the reducing triangulations, that we describe in the following section.
    We will use these metrics as follows. See Figure 1. In the statement of Proposition 5, the
surface with boundary Σ is obtained from the surface S by removing k ≥ 1 open disks (whose
closures are pairwise-disjoint). The interior Σ̊ of Σ is then homeomorphic to the punctured
surface that one would obtain by removing k points from S. In the proof of Proposition 5,
we will equip Σ̊ with a hyperbolic metric such as described above. We stress that this metric
is not defined outside of Σ̊.

2.4    Reducing triangulations

that makes no bad turn, and is still not reduced.

   This section closely follows the presentation of [10, Section 3]. A triangulation T is
reducing if its vertices have degree greater than or equal to eight, and if its dual graph is
bipartite. Every surface of genus g ≥ 2 without boundary admits a reducing triangulation.
Reducing triangulations support reduced walks and reduced closed walks. We shall

       Color the triangles of T red and blue so that adjacent triangles receive distinct colors. In the

       reduced (closed) walk is reduced. Importantly:

       ▶ Lemma 6 ([10], Proposition 3.1 and Proposition 3.4). In a reducing triangulation T , any
       two homotopic reduced walks are equal. Also, any two freely homotopic, non-contractible,
       reduced closed walks are equal.

       ▶ Lemma 7 ([10], Proposition 3.7). Let C be a closed walk of length n in a reducing
       triangulation T . One may compute a reduced closed walk freely homotopic to C in O(n) time.

          Lemma 6 will be used in the proof of Proposition 5. Lemma 7 will be used in the proof of
       Theorem 4. A statement similar to Lemma 7 holds for reduced walks (the ones not closed),
       but we will not need it.

       2.5    Patch systems and perturbations
       Let M be a graph cellularly embedded on a surface S. We present an adaptation of the strip
       systems used by Akitaya, Fulek, and Tóth [1] (and others, see .e.g [11]). Our presentation
       follows the one of Colin de Verdière, Despré, and Dubois [10, Section 2.2]. See Figure 3.
       The patch system Σ of M is a surface that can be obtained from S by first filling up any
       boundary component of S (attaching a closed disk to it), and then by removing an open
       disk from the interior of every face of M . The patch system Σ is a surface with boundary
       homotopically equivalent to M , usually thought of as a “closed neighborhood” of M in S.
       By construction, the boundary components of Σ correspond to the faces of M . We equip
       Σ with a collection of pairwise-disjoint simple arcs between its boundary components: one
       arc a for each edge e of M , where a crosses e once and does not intersect M anywhere else.
       Those arcs divide the interior of Σ into open disks, one for each vertex of M .

       We usually think of Σ as a “closed neighborhood” of M . (Right) The arcs of Σ.

       every disk of Σ as a collection of simple paths, and where every two such paths intersect at
       most once in the disk. We retain from γ only two things: the sequence of arcs of Σ crossed
       by γ and, for every arc a of Σ, the order in the crossings between γ and a occur along a.
       Dually, we retain a closed walk C in M and, for every edge e of M , a linear order ≺e on the

▶ Lemma 8. Let Σ be the patch system of a graph M cellularly embedded on a surface S.
Let C be a collection of closed walks in M . Let Γ be a perturbation of C with a minimum
number of self-crossings. If C has no spur, then Γ has iΣ (C) self-crossings.

▶ Lemma 9. Let M be a graph of size m cellularly embedded on a surface S. Let Σ be
the patch system of M . Let C be a collection of closed walks of length n in M . Let Γ be a
perturbation of C. One may compute the number of self-crossings of Γ in O(m + n log n)
time.

Proof. One must count the number of self-crossings of Γ within each disk of the patch
system Σ. There is an immediate reduction to the following problem. Fix n ≥ 2. Consider a
matching of the set [n], represented by its set E of edges. Write every edge e ∈ E as e = ij,
where i and j are the vertices of e, and i < j. Say that an edge ij ∈ E crosses an other edge
uv ∈ E if i < u < j < v, up to exchanging ij with uv. Let ⊥E be the number of unordered
pairs of edges of E that cross. Our problem is to compute ⊥E. Assuming that E is a perfect
matching, we claim that we can compute ⊥E in O(n log n) time.
    To prove this claim, we apply a divide-and-conquer strategy. The base cases (small values
of n) are trivial. In general, we consider the unique k ∈ [n] for which exactly ⌈n/2⌉ edges
uv ∈ E satisfy v ≤ k. We partition E into three sets E0 , E1 , E2 as follows. An edge uv ∈ E
belongs to E0 if it satisfies v ≤ k. It belongs to E1 if it satisfies k < u. And it belongs to E2
otherwise, that is if u ≤ k < v. By definition of k, each one of the sets E0 , E1 , E2 contains
at most ⌈n/2⌉ edges. For every l ≤ k, we let ω(l) be the number of edges uv ∈ E0 that
satisfy u < l < v. For every l > k, we let ω(l) be the number of edges uv ∈ E1 that satisfy

 3     A property of reducing triangulations
In this section we prove Proposition 5, which we recall:

▶ Proposition 5. Let T be a reducing triangulation of an orientable surface S of genus g ≥ 2
without boundary. Let Σ be the surface obtained from S by removing an open disk from
each face of T . Let C be a collection of reduced closed walks in the 1-skeleton of T . Then
iS (C) = iΣ (C).

   The proof uses classical arguments, and adapts the proof of [10, Proposition 4.3]. First,
we review the necessary background.

          The following gives a sufficient condition for two primitive closed curves to cross each
       other minimally. It is a classical fact, very similar to [13, Lemma 4].

       ▶ Lemma 11. On a surface S of genus g ≥ 2 without boundary, consider two primitive
       closed curves c and d (possibly homotopic) in general position. If in the universal cover of S,
       no lift of c crosses a lift of d more than once, then c and d cross each other minimally.

          The following gives a sufficient condition for a single primitive closed curve to cross itself
       minimally. It is easily derived from Lemma 10 and Lemma 11. It is also an immediate
       consequence of the result of Hass and Scott [17, Theorem 3.5].

       ▶ Lemma 12. On a surface S of genus g ≥ 2 without boundary, consider a primitive closed
       curve c in general position. If in the universal cover of S, the lifts of c are injective and do
       not cross more than once, then c crosses itself minimally.

       Proof of Lemma 12. Let p be the number of self-crossings of c. Consider two parallel copies
       c1 and c2 of c in general position in a neighborhood of c. By construction, there are 2p
       crossings between c1 and c2 (there would be 4p crossings if we also counted the self-crossings
       of c1 and those of c2 ). A lift of c1 cannot cross a lift of c2 more than once, so 2p = i∗S (c1 , c2 )
       by Lemma 11. We have i∗S (c1 , c2 ) = 2iS (c) by Lemma 10, since c is primitive.                   ◀
